name: Business Management
notes: Source: FBLA 2025-2026 Competitive Events Guidelines, Business Management (Updated August 2025), hosted at https://www.middletonfbla.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Business-Management_Guidelines25-26.pdf (fbla.org returned 403 to fetch). Official format is an objective test plus an interactive role play (Role Play category), not a pure case study; group is set to case per the assignment. Sub areas and test weights come from the guideline's Study Guide (Business Environment 15, Management Types 25, Business Finance 15, Operations 15, Strategic Management 30). Questions are original practice items; calculations use U.S. conventions.

questions.q: A plant manager compares weekly output to a 5,000-unit standard, finds output 8% short, and orders a root-cause review of the shortfall. Which management function is the manager primarily performing?
questions.explain: Comparing results to a standard and taking corrective action is the controlling function. Planning sets the standard; organizing and staffing come before performance is measured.

questions.q: A software company forms a team with a fixed start date, a fixed budget, and one deliverable: a mobile app launch in nine months. Which type of management is being applied?
questions.explain: A temporary effort with a defined scope, budget, and deliverable is project management. Change management focuses on people adopting new processes.

questions.q: A company's balance sheet shows total assets of $240,000 and total liabilities of $90,000. Using the accounting equation, what is owners' equity?
questions.explain: Equity equals assets minus liabilities: $240,000 minus $90,000 is $150,000. The trap is reporting total assets or liabilities as equity.

questions.q: In operations management, which term best describes the network of organizations that moves a product from raw material suppliers through manufacturers and distributors to the final customer?
questions.explain: A supply chain is the network of suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, and retailers that moves a product to the customer. A sales funnel describes how prospects become buyers.

questions.q: A manager must decide how many new employees to hire. Before writing job postings, HR must document what each position requires in duties, skills, and working conditions. What is this step called?
questions.explain: Job analysis gathers the duties, skills, and conditions for a position and comes before recruiting. Appraisal and orientation happen later in the employee lifecycle.

questions.q: A company sells monthly subscription boxes directly to consumers through its website and bypasses retail stores. Which business model is it using?
questions.explain: Selling straight to end users without intermediaries is a direct-to-consumer model. Wholesale sells to resellers, and franchising and licensing grant rights to others.

questions.q: A company spends $50,000 cash to buy new manufacturing equipment. On the statement of cash flows, under which activity is this outflow reported?
questions.explain: Purchases of long-term assets such as equipment are investing activities. This transaction involves cash, so it is not a non-cash activity.

questions.q: A bakery measures how many loaves its staff produces per labour hour and tracks the figure monthly to find efficiency gains. Which operations concept is being measured?
questions.explain: Output per unit of input, such as labour hours, is productivity. Liquidity and solvency are financial measures, and profitability measures earnings.

questions.q: A board approves a five-year plan to enter two new international markets and reallocate capital accordingly. Which type of plan is this?
questions.explain: Long-range plans that set overall direction and allocate major resources are strategic. Tactical plans are mid-range, and operational plans are short-term and specific.

questions.q: A firm buys fire insurance on its warehouse so that a loss would be covered financially. Which risk management response is this?
questions.explain: Shifting the financial consequence of a loss to an insurer is risk transfer. Avoidance would mean not operating the warehouse; reduction would mean installing sprinklers.

questions.q: A small manufacturer disputes warranty terms on machinery it sold. Which U.S. law primarily governs contracts for the sale of goods?
questions.explain: UCC Article 2 governs sales of goods in the U.S. The other laws cover wages, antitrust, and workplace safety.

questions.q: A retailer maps every activity needed to fulfill an online order, from receiving to delivery, and looks for steps that add no value. Which concept is the retailer applying?
questions.explain: Mapping and improving linked activities that turn inputs into outputs is business process management. The other choices are different disciplines.

questions.q: A manager checks the quality of incoming raw materials before production begins so defective inputs never reach the line. Which type of control is this?
questions.explain: Feedforward (preliminary) control anticipates problems before work starts. Feedback control evaluates results after the fact, and concurrent control monitors work as it happens.

questions.q: An HR department is introducing a new time-tracking system and expects employee resistance. Which management approach helps people adjust to the new process?
questions.explain: Change management plans for and supports people through a change in processes or systems. The other choices cover different areas.

questions.q: A company's current ratio is 0.8 and managers worry about paying bills due in 30 days. Which concept is most directly at issue?
questions.explain: Liquidity is the ability to meet short-term obligations. A current ratio below 1.0 means current assets do not cover current liabilities. Leverage concerns long-term debt.

questions.q: A furniture maker switches from one distant overseas supplier to two regional suppliers and cuts average lead time from 12 weeks to 3 weeks. Which effect on performance is most likely?
choices: Faster response to demand and fewer stockouts
Lower product quality from using more suppliers
questions.explain: Shorter lead times let the firm react to demand faster, so it can hold less safety stock and still avoid stockouts. Carrying costs usually fall, not rise, and nothing in the change implies lower quality or more debt.

questions.q: A call centre's goal is to cut the number of customers who have to call back about the same problem. Which metric best tracks progress toward that goal?
questions.explain: First-contact resolution rate measures the share of issues solved on the first call, which is what drives repeat calls down. Average handle time measures speed, and pushing it down can work against resolution.

questions.q: A manufacturer sells in several countries and must change its product labelling for each market's rules. Which environmental factor is most directly affecting its operations?
questions.explain: Differing labelling rules across countries are part of the global legal and regulatory environment. Demographics and technology are not the direct driver here.

questions.q: A company builds a searchable repository where employees store lessons learned from past projects and share best practices. Which management type is this?
questions.explain: Capturing, storing, and sharing organizational know-how is knowledge management.

questions.q: A company sets a goal of raising market share by 4 points in 12 months and chooses the tactics to reach it. Which management function does this represent?
questions.explain: Setting objectives and choosing the means to reach them is planning. Controlling comes later when results are compared to the plan.

questions.q: A company reports net income of $120,000, yet its cash balance fell during the year. Which statement best explains the difference?
choices: Net income always equals cash flow
Accrual accounting records revenue and expenses when earned or incurred, so timing differs from cash movement
questions.explain: Under accrual accounting, net income and cash flow can differ in timing. Depreciation is a non-cash expense, and dividends are not operating expenses.

questions.q: Which statement about a business process is most accurate?
choices: It transforms inputs into outputs through a sequence of linked activities
It is a one-time project with a fixed budget and end date
It is a financial statement that summarizes operations
It is a single department that handles one business function
questions.explain: A business process is a set of linked activities that turns inputs into outputs. A one-time effort with a fixed end date is a project, and a department is an organizational unit, not a process.

questions.q: A CEO wants employees to behave ethically, so the firm adopts a written code of conduct, trains staff on it, and rewards compliance. Which element of managerial ethics is being built?
questions.explain: A written code, training, and rewards for compliance form a formal ethics program, which shapes the ethical climate. Philanthropy is giving to outside causes, a social audit measures social responsibility performance, and ethical relativism is a philosophy, not a program.

questions.q: A hospital standardizes its patient intake forms and tracks error rates against a target so that defects drop. Which management type is most directly involved?
questions.explain: Standardizing processes and measuring defect rates against targets is quality management.

questions.q: A U.S. business decides to incorporate rather than remain a sole proprietorship. What is the most important legal consequence for the owners?
choices: Owners' personal assets are fully exposed to business debts
Owners pay taxes only at the entity level
Owners have limited liability for business debts
Owners lose the right to vote on decisions
questions.explain: Incorporation generally limits shareholders' personal liability to their investment. The other choices misstate the effect of incorporating.

questions.q: A company earns revenue of $800,000, has cost of goods sold of $500,000, and operating expenses of $200,000. What is gross profit?
questions.explain: Gross profit is revenue minus cost of goods sold: $800,000 minus $500,000 is $300,000. Subtracting operating expenses gives operating income, not gross profit.

questions.q: A company relies on a single supplier for a critical component. A flood shuts that supplier down and halts production for weeks. Which supply chain impact best describes this event?
choices: The bullwhip effect from distorted demand signals
Inventory shrinkage from theft or damage
A capacity bottleneck inside its own plant
Supply disruption caused by single sourcing
questions.explain: Relying on one supplier (single sourcing) leaves no backup when that supplier fails, so a local event halts production. The bullwhip effect is demand distortion along the chain, shrinkage is lost stock, and the constraint here is outside the plant, not inside it.

questions.q: A manager measures staff against monthly targets and then corrects any gaps. Which sequence correctly describes the control process?
choices: Hire staff, train staff, evaluate staff, dismiss staff
Set standards, measure performance, compare to standards, take corrective action
Forecast demand, buy inventory, sell product, close books
Draft mission, write vision, list values, publish
questions.explain: The control process is: set standards, measure performance, compare results to standards, and take corrective action where needed.

questions.q: A company is worried about legal compliance and wants a formal approach to identify, rate, and respond to threats to its objectives. Which management type fits best?
questions.explain: Identifying, assessing, and responding to threats to objectives is risk management.

questions.q: A company's CEO states that the firm will be the most trusted brand in its industry within ten years. Which element of strategic management does this statement represent?
questions.explain: A vision statement describes the desired future state. A code of conduct governs behaviour, and a budget and organization chart serve other purposes.

questions.q: A company compares its budgeted expenses for the year to actual expenses to find out why profits fell. Which financial tool is it using?
questions.explain: Comparing budget to actual results to explain differences is variance analysis.

questions.q: Why do companies study their business processes?
choices: To meet a legal requirement for incorporation
To find waste, reduce cycle time, and improve quality and cost
To shift all operating risk to suppliers
To replace the need for a strategic plan
questions.explain: Studying processes exposes waste, delays, and defects so the firm can cut cycle time and cost and raise quality. It is not a legal requirement and does not remove risk or replace strategy.

questions.q: A manager plans to change how a team schedules its daily work and expects pushback. Which approach best reduces conflict and builds support before the change?
choices: Announce the change by email on the day it starts
Make the change mandatory and tie it to discipline
Involve employees in planning and explain the reasons for the change
Delay the change until resistance fades on its own
questions.explain: Involving people and explaining why builds understanding and ownership, which lowers resistance. Surprise announcements and threats raise resistance, and waiting does not address its causes.

questions.q: A retailer records each customer's purchases, preferences, and service history to tailor offers. Which management type is this?
questions.explain: Using customer data to manage and personalize relationships is customer relationship management.

questions.q: A multinational firm faces a sudden change in exchange rates that raises the cost of its imported parts. Which environment is most directly involved?
questions.explain: Exchange rates and input costs are part of the economic environment. The other environments do not drive this change directly.

questions.q: Management theory lists four managerial functions. Which set is correct?
questions.explain: The four functions are planning, organizing, leading, and controlling. The other sets mix in activities that fall within these functions.

questions.q: A company has $60,000 in current assets and $40,000 in current liabilities. What is its working capital?
questions.explain: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities: $60,000 minus $40,000 is $20,000.

questions.q: A manager wants to measure the time from receiving an order to delivering the product. Which measure is this?
questions.explain: The elapsed time from order to delivery is lead time (or cycle time). The other measures are financial ratios.

questions.q: Managers decide which tasks to group into departments and who reports to whom. Which managerial function is this?
questions.explain: Grouping tasks and setting reporting lines is organizing.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a sole proprietorship?
choices: A business owned by shareholders with limited liability
A business owned by one person with no legal separation from the owner, who is personally liable for its debts
A business owned by a partnership of at least two investors and taxed as a corporation
A non-profit organization exempt from income tax
questions.explain: A sole proprietorship has one owner who is personally liable for business debts. The other choices describe corporations, partnerships, and non-profits.

questions.q: A company sets a goal to cut its product defect rate from 4% to 1% within a year, using standardized measurement and continuous improvement. Which approach is this?
questions.explain: Total quality management focuses on continuous improvement and measured quality outcomes across the organization.

questions.q: A company's accounts receivable turnover is low, so customers take a long time to pay. Which action most directly addresses the liquidity concern?
choices: Tighten credit terms and follow up on overdue invoices
Increase the dividend payout to shareholders
Offer longer payment terms to new buyers
Buy new equipment with cash on hand
questions.explain: Tightening credit and collecting overdue invoices speeds cash inflows. The other choices reduce cash or slow collections.

questions.q: A company sets inventory levels using just-in-time principles. What is the main benefit?
choices: It requires the largest warehouse space
It removes the need for suppliers
It cuts carrying costs and waste by receiving inventory close to when it is needed
questions.explain: JIT reduces carrying costs and waste by timing deliveries to need. It does not eliminate demand uncertainty or suppliers.

questions.q: A company links pay to goals that each employee and manager set together. Which motivational approach is this?
questions.explain: Management by objectives sets jointly agreed goals and ties rewards to achieving them.

questions.q: Managers analyze the number of potential customers, their ages, and income levels before choosing store locations. Which environment is most directly analyzed?
questions.explain: Population size, age, and income are demographic factors.

questions.q: A company keeps a second qualified vendor for a key part because its main vendor could go bankrupt. Which risk response is this?
questions.explain: Having a backup source lowers the likelihood and impact of a supply failure, which is risk reduction.

questions.q: Orders pass through three steps in sequence. Step 1 can handle 60 orders per hour, step 2 can handle 40, and step 3 can handle 50. What is the most the whole process can complete per hour?
choices: 60 orders, set by the fastest step
50 orders, the average of the three steps
150 orders, the sum of the three steps
40 orders, set by the bottleneck step
questions.explain: In a sequential process, output is capped by the slowest step (the bottleneck), here 40 per hour. Faster steps only build a queue in front of step 2.

questions.q: A firm's net profit margin is 6% and its sales are $2,000,000. What is its net income?
questions.explain: Net income is margin times sales: 6% of $2,000,000 is $120,000.

questions.q: Leaders want an organizational culture that supports open communication. Which step most directly supports this in the leading function?
choices: Route all concerns to senior staff through formal written reports
Hold fewer team meetings so staff can focus on their tasks
Communicate openly, model the behaviour, and recognize staff who raise concerns
Post a list of company values and leave behaviour to each team
questions.explain: Open culture grows when leaders share information, model the behaviour themselves, and reward people who speak up. Formal-only channels, fewer meetings, and posters without action all discourage open communication.

questions.q: Which human resources activity most directly determines the skills a business needs before it recruits?
questions.explain: Human resource planning forecasts the skills and headcount the business needs, which guides recruiting.

questions.q: A firm groups employees into marketing, finance, and production units, each reporting to a senior manager. Which organizational design is this?
questions.explain: Grouping by business function is a functional structure. Product structures group by product line.

questions.q: A company cuts its suppliers from 40 to 8 to gain volume discounts and simpler management. Which risk should managers monitor most closely?
choices: A higher number of quality audits
Dependence on fewer suppliers that may raise disruption risk
An increase in the number of contracts
questions.explain: Fewer suppliers can bring discounts but increase the impact of any single disruption.

questions.q: Results will be reviewed every week against the plan, with exceptions reported immediately. Which part of the control process is being emphasized?
choices: Measuring performance and comparing it to standards
questions.explain: Weekly review against the plan, with exceptions flagged, is the measure-and-compare step. The standards already exist (the plan), and corrective action comes after a gap is found.

questions.q: A company issues $100,000 of bonds at 5% interest. Annual interest expense is $5,000 regardless of profit. Which term describes this obligation?
questions.explain: Interest on debt is a fixed financing cost that creates leverage. It is not an operating expense, a dividend, or depreciation.

questions.q: A company uses continuous improvement in its operations. Which is the best example?
choices: Replacing an entire production line in one major overhaul
Inspecting every finished unit before it ships
Benchmarking against a rival once and filing the report
Regularly reviewing a process and making small changes that reduce waste over time
questions.explain: Continuous improvement (kaizen) is ongoing, incremental refinement of a process. A one-time overhaul is radical change, end-of-line inspection catches defects without improving the process, and a one-off benchmark is not continuous.

questions.q: A market has low entry barriers and many new firms can enter easily. Which competitive force is most directly described?
questions.explain: Low barriers to entry describe the threat of new entrants in Porter's five forces.

questions.q: A company's stated purpose is to provide affordable healthy food to every community it serves. Which element of strategic management is this?
questions.explain: A mission statement describes the organization's purpose and what it does for whom.

questions.q: A risk team rates each threat to its information systems, such as a data breach or a server outage, by likelihood and potential impact, then plots the results on a grid to decide which to address first. Which tool is the team using?
questions.explain: A risk matrix ranks risks by likelihood and impact so the highest-priority ones get attention first. A Gantt chart schedules tasks, a control chart tracks process variation, and a fishbone diagram traces the causes of a problem.

questions.q: A company's gross margin is 40% on sales of $500,000. What is its cost of goods sold?
questions.explain: Gross margin of 40% means COGS is 60% of sales: 0.60 times $500,000 is $300,000.

questions.q: A company has a lead time of 10 days and average daily demand of 50 units. With no safety stock, what is the reorder point?
questions.explain: Reorder point is lead-time demand: 10 days times 50 units per day is 500 units.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the four perspectives of a balanced scorecard?
choices: Financial, customer, internal business process, and learning and growth
questions.explain: The balanced scorecard uses financial, customer, internal process, and learning and growth perspectives.

questions.q: A company faces a new technology that could replace its product entirely. Which competitive force is this?
questions.explain: A product that could be replaced by a different product or technology is a threat of substitutes.

questions.q: A company's data governance policy requires personal customer information to be encrypted and access logged. Which management type is most directly involved?
questions.explain: Protecting and controlling access to information is information management.

questions.q: A company runs a push system, producing to forecast. Compared with a pull system that produces to actual orders, what is the typical drawback of push?
choices: Longer order cycle times by definition
Higher risk of excess inventory when forecasts are wrong
questions.explain: Producing to forecast can build excess inventory when demand falls short of the forecast.

questions.q: A company's flattened structure now has three approval levels instead of seven. Which organizational design change is this?
questions.explain: Reducing layers of management is flattening the structure. The other options are strategic moves, not structural changes.

questions.q: A state law requires environmental impact reports before a company can build a plant. Which environment is this?
questions.explain: Government requirements for permits and reports are part of the legal-regulatory environment.

questions.q: A manager delegates authority to team leaders. Which managerial consideration does this illustrate?
questions.explain: Delegation distributes authority and responsibility, a part of organizing.

questions.q: A consulting firm delivers $30,000 of services in December and collects the cash in January. Under accrual accounting, when is the revenue recognized?
choices: Split equally between the two months
At the end of the fiscal year
questions.explain: Accrual accounting recognizes revenue when it is earned, which is when the service is delivered in December. January, when cash arrives, would be the cash-basis answer.

questions.q: A company's cost of goods sold is $900,000 and its average inventory is $150,000. What is its inventory turnover?
questions.explain: Inventory turnover is COGS divided by average inventory: $900,000 divided by $150,000 is 6.

questions.q: Which statement describes the assumptions of Theory X management?
choices: Workers dislike work and need close supervision
Workers are motivated mainly by teamwork
questions.explain: Theory X assumes workers avoid work and need direction and control, in contrast with Theory Y.

questions.q: A CEO promises to cut carbon emissions per unit by 20%, in response to stakeholder expectations. Which environment is this most closely linked to?
questions.explain: Stakeholder expectations about environmental responsibility are part of the social environment.

questions.q: Which U.S. business form gives owners limited liability and an unlimited life that continues beyond any one owner?
questions.explain: A corporation gives limited liability and perpetual existence. Sole proprietorships and general partnerships expose owners to personal liability.

questions.q: A company's debt-to-equity ratio is 2.0. What does this indicate?
choices: It has twice as much equity as debt
It has twice as much debt as equity financing
Its assets are twice its liabilities
questions.explain: A debt-to-equity ratio of 2.0 means debt is twice equity.

questions.q: In a Gantt chart, what does a bar represent?
choices: The scheduled duration of a task
questions.explain: Each bar shows a task's start, end, and duration on a timeline.

questions.q: Which pair correctly identifies internal factors in a SWOT analysis?
questions.explain: Strengths and weaknesses are internal. Opportunities and threats are external.

questions.q: A board requires a formal succession plan for key executives. Which HR area is this?
questions.explain: Succession planning identifies future leaders and is part of human resource planning.

questions.q: A company sells goods on credit for $5,000. In the entry that records the $5,000 selling price, which account is credited?
questions.explain: The selling price is debited to accounts receivable and credited to sales revenue. Under a perpetual system a separate entry at cost debits cost of goods sold and credits inventory, but that is not the $5,000 sale entry.

questions.q: A quality team uses statistical process control charts. What is their primary purpose?
choices: To monitor whether a process stays within expected variation
questions.explain: Control charts track process variation over time to detect when a process goes out of control.

questions.q: A manager uses management by exception. What does this mean?
choices: Managers grant exceptions to policy for top performers
Managers focus on significant deviations from plan rather than routine results
questions.explain: Management by exception directs attention to significant deviations from plan.

questions.q: Which area of management is most directly responsible for making sure the firm follows federal overtime and minimum-wage rules?
questions.explain: Human resources management handles pay practices and compliance with U.S. wage and hour law, mainly the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA).

questions.q: A company's return on equity is 15% and its net income is $300,000. What is its average shareholders' equity?
questions.explain: ROE is net income divided by equity: $300,000 divided by 0.15 is $2,000,000.

questions.q: A company merges purchasing across its branches to lower unit costs. Which concept does this illustrate?
questions.explain: Spreading volume across branches lowers unit costs, which is economies of scale.

questions.q: Which managerial activity is primarily part of the staffing function?
questions.explain: Staffing covers recruiting, selecting, training, and retaining employees.

questions.q: An integrated system gives sales, production, and finance one view of customer orders and inventory. Which management type does this best reflect?
questions.explain: Integrating data across functions for decisions is information management.

questions.q: A company expanding abroad faces new tariffs on its imports. Which environment is most directly affected?
questions.explain: Tariffs are trade policy and fall within the global political and legal environment.

questions.q: A company has a current ratio of 2.5 and a quick ratio of 1.0. What does the gap suggest?
choices: A large share of current assets is inventory
Liabilities are growing faster than assets
questions.explain: The quick ratio excludes inventory, so a big gap means inventory makes up much of current assets.

questions.q: A plant can produce 1,000 units per day and produces 800. What is its capacity utilization?
questions.explain: Utilization is actual output divided by capacity: 800 divided by 1,000 is 80%.

questions.q: Which step of the strategic management process comes after strategy formulation?
questions.explain: Formulation is followed by implementation, then evaluation and control. Environmental scanning comes before formulation.

questions.q: Which term means the accounting standards used to prepare U.S. financial statements?
questions.explain: GAAP is the body of accounting standards used in the United States.

questions.q: Which statement best defines a value-added activity?
choices: An activity that increases the product's worth to the customer
Any activity performed at a supplier's facility
questions.explain: A value-added activity is one the customer would pay for. Other activities are waste to reduce.

questions.q: Which leadership style gives employees the most decision-making power?
questions.explain: Laissez-faire leaders delegate most decisions to the group. Autocratic and paternalistic styles keep decisions with the leader.

questions.q: A company buys $500 of raw materials on credit. Which account increases?
questions.explain: Buying on credit increases inventory and accounts payable. Cash is unchanged.

questions.q: A manufacturer coordinates its parts suppliers, a contract assembler, and a third-party logistics firm so that materials, production, and deliveries stay in step. Which management type is most directly applied?
questions.explain: Coordinating the flow of materials and products across suppliers, producers, and logistics partners is supply chain management.

questions.q: Before rolling out a new enterprise system, a manager shows staff how the old process causes errors and delays so they see why it has to change. In Lewin's three-step change model, which stage is this?
questions.explain: Unfreezing prepares people by showing why the current way cannot continue. Changing is the move to the new system, and refreezing locks the new way in. Benchmarking is not a Lewin stage.

questions.q: A company hedges its foreign currency exposure with financial contracts to protect earnings. Which risk response is this?
choices: Risk avoidance by exiting the market
Risk transfer to a contract counterparty
questions.explain: A currency hedge shifts part of the potential loss to the counterparty on the contract. Risk frameworks such as COSO ERM class hedging, like insurance, as transfer (sharing).

questions.q: A machine setup takes four hours and happens once per batch. Which improvement would best reduce waste from setups?
choices: Increase the batch size without changing setup
Reduce setup time with quick-changeover methods
questions.explain: Quick-changeover methods such as SMED cut setup time, which lowers the cost of each batch.

questions.q: Which section of a business plan describes what a new café will do to win and keep customers?
questions.explain: The marketing plan describes target customers, pricing, promotion, and distribution.

questions.q: An asset costs $50,000 with a $5,000 salvage value and a five-year life. Under straight-line depreciation, what is the annual expense?
questions.explain: Straight-line depreciation is (cost minus salvage) divided by life: $45,000 divided by 5 is $9,000.

questions.q: A regional sales manager sets specific monthly sales quotas for each territory for the coming quarter. Which type of plan is this?
questions.explain: Short-term, specific targets for units or people are operational plans. Strategic plans set long-range direction, and contingency plans cover what to do if something goes wrong.

questions.q: A company uses a Gantt chart and the critical path method to plan a project. What does the critical path identify?
choices: The tasks that can be delayed without delaying the project
The longest sequence of dependent tasks that sets the minimum project duration
The tasks with the highest cost
The shortest route through the task network
questions.explain: The critical path is the longest chain of dependent tasks, so it sets the shortest possible completion time; any delay on it delays the project. Tasks that can slip have slack and sit off the critical path.

vocab.def: The method by which a company creates, delivers, and captures value, such as selling direct, by franchise, or by subscription.
A business owned and operated by one person, with no legal separation between the owner and the business.
A business owned by two or more persons who share profits, losses, and management under a partnership agreement.
A legal entity separate from its owners (shareholders) that offers limited liability and continues to exist apart from any owner.
A protection under which owners are not personally responsible for the debts of the business beyond their investment.
The way a firm arranges its tasks, reporting relationships, and departments to achieve its goals, such as functional or divisional structure.
A set of standardized U.S. state laws that govern commercial transactions, including sales of goods under Article 2.
U.S. laws, including the Sherman Act and Clayton Act, that prohibit practices which restrain competition, such as price-fixing.
A competitive force in which low barriers to entry allow new firms to enter an industry and reduce existing firms' profits.
The planning, organizing, and control of a temporary effort with a defined scope, budget, schedule, and deliverable.
A structured approach to preparing, supporting, and helping people adopt a change in processes, systems, or structure.
The process of capturing, storing, sharing, and applying an organization's knowledge and best practices.
Systematic activities that ensure products and services meet defined standards, including measurement and continuous improvement.
A management approach that involves everyone in continuous improvement of quality with a focus on customer satisfaction.
The process of identifying, assessing, and responding to threats that could keep an organization from achieving its objectives.
A risk response that eliminates a risk by not engaging in the activity that creates it.
A risk response that shifts the financial consequence of a loss to another party, usually through insurance or contracts.
A strategy and set of tools used to manage interactions with customers in order to improve retention and satisfaction.
The coordination of activities that move goods and information from suppliers through manufacturers and distributors to customers.
The process of forecasting the number and type of employees a business will need and planning how to meet those needs.
The collection, storage, protection, and use of data and information systems to support business decisions.
Using financial instruments to offset the risk of price, interest rate, or currency changes.
Inspection and testing methods that detect defects so that output meets specified standards.
Identifying and developing future leaders so that key positions can be filled when they become vacant.
The sequence of analyzing the environment, formulating strategy, implementing it, and evaluating and controlling results.
A financial statement that shows a company's assets, liabilities, and owners' equity at a specific point in time.
A financial statement that reports revenues, expenses, and net income for a period of time.
A financial statement that reports cash inflows and outflows in operating, investing, and financing activities for a period.
A financial plan that estimates revenues and expenses for a future period and serves as a benchmark for control.
A company's ability to pay its short-term obligations as they come due.
Current assets minus current liabilities, a measure of short-term financial health.
An accounting method that records revenues when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of when cash changes hands.
The sales volume at which total revenue equals total costs, so the business has neither profit nor loss.
Revenue minus cost of goods sold, before operating expenses are subtracted.
The network of organizations, resources, and activities that moves a product from raw materials to the final customer.
A set of linked activities that transforms inputs into outputs to create value for a customer.
The ratio of output to the input used to produce it, such as units produced per labour hour.
The total time from placing an order to receiving the goods or completing the process.
An inventory system that receives materials only as they are needed in production, reducing carrying costs and waste.
The percentage of maximum possible output that a firm actually produces.
The number of times inventory is sold and replaced in a period, calculated as cost of goods sold divided by average inventory.
Cost advantages that a firm gains as its volume of production grows, lowering the cost per unit.
The longest sequence of dependent tasks in a project, which sets the minimum time needed to finish it.
A statement of an organization's purpose and what it does for whom.
A statement describing the future state the organization aims to achieve.
A review of a firm's internal strengths and weaknesses and external opportunities and threats.
A long-range plan that sets an organization's overall direction and allocates major resources.
A short-term, specific plan that sets the detailed actions and targets needed to carry out strategy.
The process of setting standards, measuring performance, comparing results to standards, and taking corrective action.
Control that anticipates problems before work begins, such as inspecting inputs before production.
A process in which managers and employees jointly set goals and link rewards to achieving them.
A performance framework measuring financial, customer, internal process, and learning and growth perspectives.
A measurable value that shows how effectively an organization is achieving a key objective.
A management approach that focuses attention on significant deviations from plan rather than routine results.
The management function of grouping tasks, assigning authority, and establishing reporting relationships.
The management function of recruiting, selecting, training, and retaining employees.
The standards of right and wrong that guide managers' decisions and behaviour toward employees, customers, and society.
A leadership style in which leaders give employees wide freedom to make decisions with little direction.
A management assumption that workers dislike work and need close supervision and control.
A written document describing a business's goals, strategy, market, operations, and financial projections.
